newsitem.title: USA: Simulation of ill-fated TWA 800 set for Monday.
newsitem.headline: Simulation of ill-fated TWA 800 set for Monday.

text.p: A simulation of last year's tragic TWA Flight 800 is scheduled for Monday, National Transportation Safety Board Chairman Jim Hall said on Sunday.

The test will involve a Boeing 747 loaded with more than 150 sensors in an effort to gain more clues into the crash that killed 230 people last July 17, shortly after take-off from New York's John F. Kennedy airport bound for Paris.
Investigators agree the explosion of the plane's center fuel tank caused the disintegration of the plane off Long Island, but what touched off the blast is still undetermined.
"The whole center tank will be very highly instrumented," Hall said in an interview on CNN's Late Edition.

Temperatures in the tank will be monitored as the plane reaches the altitude at which the explosion occurred, he said. Investigators also will try to understand how possible movement of the tank might have affected the build-up of vapors.
Hall said there were potential dangers in the experiment, but the experts involved were taking suitable precautions.

"There is an element of danger. Now that is supposed to be taken out of the equation by the people that have knowledge in this area, but we are very, very careful, obviously, in putting this simulation together," he said.
The FBI says it has not found any evidence that a bomb or a missile caused the blast, although it has not totally excluded the possibility.
The simulation will help the NTSB determine how explosive the mix of fuel and air fumes were in the nearly empty center tank, and how much energy might have been needed to trigger the explosion.

That information could provide clues on the viability of other theories, such as whether a low energy spark from another piece of equipment was enough to ignite the tank or whether investigators should be looking for a much bigger source of energy.

The simulations also may help settle a debate between the NTSB and the Federal Aviation Administration on whether adding cooler fuel to the center tank before flight might avoid similar accidents in the future.
The FAA and the airline industry are skeptical of the NTSB's proposal to add fuel, saying the fumes in the tank would still be potentially explosive.

Much of the disagreement hinges on whether the center tank vibrates enough in flight to add to the vapor's flammability. The NTSB says the tank doesn't normally vibrate that much, so the addition of cooler fuel could make a big difference.
